name: spinach ricotta
instructions:
Two variants sharing the spinach-plus-ricotta identity — variant A is the cooked dairy pasta sauce, variant B is the raw-blended vegan version (Beth Hornback / Pass the Plants) that also functions as a filling for baked dishes. Different techniques, related flavor register.

=== VARIANT A — DAIRY (COOKED SKILLET SAUCE) ===

A ricotta-and-greens pasta built on seared ricotta (or food-processed cottage cheese) + food-processor-chopped greens + cream + garlic. Nutmeg and red chili flakes carry the flavor — more so than the greens themselves (see notes).

INGREDIENTS:
- pasta
- olive oil
- garlic
- ricotta cheese and/or cottage cheese (see notes on the swap)
- spinach, parsley, mixed greens (or really any greens — see notes)
- heavy whipping cream (as much as needed to bring the sauce together)
- nutmeg (to taste — critical, see notes)
- red chili flakes (to taste — critical, see notes)
- cayenne pepper
- lemon juice and lemon zest (to taste)
- pasta water (reserved from cooking)
- salt, black pepper

PROCEDURE:
1. Cook the pasta in well-salted water. Reserve some pasta water before draining.
2. In a separate pan, cook the garlic in olive oil until fragrant (don't brown).
3. SEAR/COOK THE RICOTTA (OR FOOD-PROCESSED COTTAGE CHEESE): add the ricotta (or cottage cheese run through a food processor to smooth it out) to the garlicky oil. Let it cook against the hot pan — searing gives it a slightly toasted, more concentrated flavor rather than reading as raw cheese.
4. Chop the greens (spinach + parsley + mixed greens) in a food processor. Fold them in after the ricotta has seared.
5. Add heavy cream as necessary to bring it together into a proper sauce.
6. Season with nutmeg, red chili flakes, and cayenne — all to taste. Nutmeg and chili flakes are the load-bearing flavors here (see notes).
7. Finish with lemon juice and lemon zest to taste.
8. Add the cooked pasta and enough reserved pasta water to loosen the sauce and get it to coat the pasta.
9. Salt and black pepper to taste.

=== VARIANT B — VEGAN (RAW-BLENDED BASE, BETH HORNBACK / PASS THE PLANTS) ===

Raw-blended vegan analog. Two use cases: as a raw pasta sauce (my tested use), or as a filling for baked dishes like lasagna / calzones / stuffed shells (Beth's intended use, untested by me).

BASE INGREDIENTS (Beth's default):
- 1 cup raw cashews
- 1 (12-oz) package firm or extra-firm tofu, drained (not pressed — moisture helps consistency)
- 2 cups fresh baby spinach (or 1 cup frozen)
- 1/4 cup fresh basil leaves
- 2 cloves garlic
- 1 tsp salt
- 1 tsp light miso paste (white, yellow, or chickpea miso)
- 2 tbsp nutritional yeast

ADDITIONS FOR THE PASTA-SAUCE USE CASE (borrowed from variant A's flavor axis):
- LEMON ZEST + LEMON JUICE (to taste)
- NUTMEG (a pinch)
- RED CHILI FLAKES (a pinch)
- PORCINI MUSHROOM POWDER (small amount — breaks up the miso/nutritional yeast monotone, see notes)
- DRIED THYME (confirmed successful in the pasta version)

PROCEDURE:
1. In a food processor (NOT a blender — see notes), pulse the cashews, garlic, MISO, salt, and nutritional yeast until fine and crumbly. If doing the pasta-sauce use case, add the porcini powder here too.
2. Add the tofu, spinach, and basil. If doing the pasta-sauce use case, add the lemon zest, lemon juice, nutmeg, chili flakes, and thyme now. Pulse until combined — no large tofu or spinach pieces detectable.
3. USE AS PASTA SAUCE: warm the base briefly in a pan (don't simmer), thin with pasta water, toss with cooked pasta immediately.
4. USE AS FILLING (LASAGNA / CALZONES / STUFFED SHELLS): use raw straight out of the food processor as filling; the downstream bake does the cooking. Beth's intended use; I haven't personally tested this yet in something like lasagna.
notes:
=== NUTMEG AND CHILI FLAKES ARE CRITICAL — MORE SO THAN THE GREENS ===

The greens carry visual/textural weight but the FLAVOR of the dish (variant A, or variant B in pasta-sauce mode) is nutmeg + red chili flakes. Without them the sauce reads flat and generic-creamy-cheese. With them it reads as a proper composed dish. Add both to taste — don't skimp. If you're going to under-do anything in this recipe, let it be the greens; if you're going to over-do anything, let it be the nutmeg and chili flakes.

=== VARIANT A NOTES ===

SEAR/COOK THE RICOTTA — DON'T LEAVE IT RAW: cooking the ricotta (or food-processed cottage cheese) against the hot garlicky pan is a real technique step, not just heating. Searing gives the cheese a slightly toasted, more concentrated flavor that reads as an actual cooked component rather than as a raw dairy dollop stirred in. Skip this and the sauce reads flat and dairy-forward without the cheese pulling its weight.

RICOTTA OR FOOD-PROCESSED COTTAGE CHEESE — INTERCHANGEABLE: either works. Ricotta is smoother out of the tub. Cottage cheese needs a food processor pass first to smooth out the curds — unprocessed cottage cheese would give you visible grainy curds in the sauce, which reads wrong. Same swap-friendly cheese-role framing as tomato-tart's bulk cheese role.

CREAM AS NEEDED FOR A REAL SAUCE: how much cream depends on how the ricotta + greens land — sometimes the mixture is already spreadable, sometimes it needs real thinning. Add enough cream to bring it to a sauce consistency that will coat the pasta once you toss with pasta water. Not a fixed amount; go by feel.

PASTA WATER TO LOOSEN AT THE END: reserve pasta water before draining. Add enough to bring the sauce to coating consistency after the pasta goes in. Standard italian pasta-sauce move — the starchy water helps the sauce cling.

=== VARIANT B NOTES — RAW-BLENDED VEGAN BASE ===

SOURCE: Beth Hornback, Pass the Plants blog. Base recipe (cashews + tofu + spinach + basil + garlic + salt + miso + nutritional yeast) is Beth's default. My extension for the pasta-sauce use case adds lemon/nutmeg/chili/porcini/thyme to align the flavor register with variant A.

NO COOK STEP — RAW BLENDED BASE: nothing cooks in variant B. Cooking happens downstream — either the pan-warm-and-toss for pasta use, or the oven bake if used as a filling in lasagna / calzones / stuffed shells / zucchini roll-ups.

GENERAL RULE FOR BLENDED-TOFU SAUCES — WARM, DON'T SIMMER: if using as a pasta sauce, warm briefly in a pan and toss with hot pasta immediately. Don't try to simmer or reduce a blended-tofu sauce — it doesn't thicken further, doesn't caramelize, and gets grainy if pushed hard. Different from dairy sauces (variant A) which benefit from a real cook / sear step.

USE CASES — WHAT I'VE ACTUALLY DONE:
- VARIANT B AS PASTA SAUCE: tested — variant B with the pasta-sauce additions, thinned with pasta water, tossed with cooked spaghetti. Works well.
- VARIANT B AS LASAGNA / CALZONE / STUFFED-SHELL FILLING: intended default per Beth's original framing, but I haven't personally tested it yet. When I try it, log the result here. Whether the pasta-sauce additions (lemon/nutmeg/chili/porcini/thyme) also work in filling applications is untested — might be good, might not; I don't know.

MISO GOES IN THE FOOD PROCESSOR PHASE — DON'T TRY TO FOLD IT IN LATER: the miso paste needs to go in during the food-processor phase (with the cashews + garlic + salt + nutritional yeast). Don't try to fold it in during a later skillet phase or off-heat mixing — this is a low-liquid recipe and there's not enough sauce moisture for miso paste to disperse evenly if added late. You'll end up with concentrated miso blobs in an otherwise-bland matrix.

TOFU CHOICE — SILKEN VS FIRM: silken gives a very creamy sauce-like final texture (good for the pasta-sauce use case). Firm gives a chunkier, more ricotta-like texture (closer to what dairy ricotta would do; better for filling applications). Beth's original calls for firm or extra-firm; either fine.

AUG 24 2026 LOGBOOK — FIRM + PRESSED TOFU IN THE PASTA-SAUCE USE CASE (CONJECTURE): tried firm + pressed tofu today in the pasta-sauce use case (rather than silken). Result: basically as good as silken, though silken is obviously creamier. At some point I had to hydrate the firm version with HEAVY CREAM to bring it together (water might have worked instead — untested).

CONJECTURE from this cook (log entry, not a rule):
- Firm tofu version probably fits BETTER for STUFFING PEPPERS (matches the ricotta-like texture that stuffing applications want).
- Firm tofu version probably pairs BETTER with THICKER NOODLES (the chunkier sauce matches thicker pasta shapes; silken's creamy sauce is more at home with thinner noodles).
- Silken still wins for a smooth-sauce-over-thin-pasta target.
All conjecture until re-tested. Log further attempts here.

CASHEWS MATTER MORE WITH FIRMER TOFU: the cashews add creamy body that firm tofu doesn't provide. With silken tofu (already creamy), you could probably get away with fewer cashews. With firm/extra-firm, keep the full amount.

PORCINI MUSHROOM POWDER — BREAKS UP THE MISO / NUTRITIONAL-YEAST MONOTONE: miso and nutritional yeast together are the classic 'vegan glutamate bomb' — they cover the same savory-cheesy register from slightly different angles and can read one-note when it's just those two carrying the umami. Porcini adds a different kind of savory depth (woodsy-mushroom) that complements without duplicating. Turns 'flat processed-savory' into 'layered savory.' Consistent with the standing feedback-vegan-glutamate memory principle.

DRIED HERB ADDITIONS FOR VARIANT B: dried thyme confirmed successful in the pasta-sauce version. Herbes de provence and oregano are both untested but plausible extensions of the herb axis — herbes de provence would layer with the thyme (already thyme-inclusive) and add sage/lavender/rosemary background; oregano would push more italian-classical alongside the red chili flakes.

NOT-CASHEW SUBSTITUTIONS (BETH'S NOTES FOR NUT ALLERGIES):
- PEPITAS (raw shelled pumpkin seeds): tested by her, worked well.
- SKIP CASHEWS ENTIRELY + DOUBLE THE TOFU: also works per her; simpler.

=== NUT AXIS — CASHEWS ONLY (STRICTER THAN PESTO) ===

Hardened rule (advanced further from the previous conjecture): NUTS DETERMINED BY TOFU TYPE, AND WHEN NUTS ARE USED, CASHEWS ARE THE ONLY CORRECT NUT.

- VARIANT A (TRADITIONAL DAIRY): NO nuts. Dairy ricotta / cottage cheese + cream carries the body; nuts just clutter.
- VARIANT B WITH FIRM / DRAINED TOFU: NO nuts. Firm tofu already provides the chunky ricotta-like texture.
- VARIANT B WITH SILKEN TOFU: CASHEWS YES, other nuts NO. Silken tofu is smooth all the way through, so cashews create the chunky-ricotta-like texture the dish wants.

CASHEWS ARE THE ONLY CORRECT NUT — EVERYTHING ELSE IS CLASHING:
- SUNFLOWER SEEDS: too protein-rich. Push the base into a heavier, more protein-forward register than the dish wants. Clashing.
- PINE NUTS: pull the flavor in a different direction. Don't fit the miso + nutritional yeast + garlic + basil register the way cashews do. Clashing.
- ALMONDS: clashing. Peeling first (a valid remediation elsewhere) doesn't rescue them here — still wrong.
- WALNUTS: clashing. Toasting first (a valid remediation elsewhere) doesn't rescue them here — still wrong.

LIKE PESTO BUT WITH MORE CONSTRAINTS: pesto has similar nut preferences (pine nuts / cashews / sunflower work; almonds/walnuts less good) but is more forgiving — pesto tolerates several nut choices. This dish is stricter: cashews are the specific right answer for variant B with silken; everything else drops out.

UNLIKE PESTO — NUTS ARE OPTIONAL: pesto requires nuts (structural). This recipe doesn't — the rule above (nuts only with silken) means nuts get skipped whenever the base already has structural texture. Even with silken, Beth's 'skip cashews + double the tofu' path is fine if you don't want any nuts.

STORES WELL — FRIDGE + FREEZER: fridge covered up to a week. Freezes well — worth doubling and freezing half for future lasagna, calzones, or stuffed shells. If doubling, make in TWO batches (too much for a food processor at once, per Beth's note).

=== PASTA SHAPE — RIGATONI / PENNE PREFERRED (ESPECIALLY BAKED); SPAGHETTI ONLY WITH SILKEN + NO NUTS ===

- BEST: RIGATONI and PENNE. Especially good when the dish is BAKED (see BAKED IN THE OVEN note below) — the tubes hold the chunky ricotta/tofu base cleanly and take a proper cheese-top-melt.
- OK: FETTUCCINE — edible but not the pick.
- WEIRD: SPAGHETTI — usually reads wrong. EXCEPTION: if you're doing variant B with SILKEN tofu and CLOSE TO NO NUTS (a flat cream sauce format), spaghetti is fine — that combination lands as a smooth-cream-over-thin-pasta target, which is a legitimate direction. Just don't do spaghetti with a chunky ricotta or firm-tofu base; the sauce won't grip.

=== UNLIKE PESTO — CAN BE BAKED IN THE OVEN WITH LOTS OF CHEESE ===

Unlike pesto (which is served raw / warm-off-heat), spinach ricotta CAN be baked in the oven with a generous cheese top layer. Applies to both variants — the ricotta / cashew-tofu base holds up to the bake and takes a proper melted-cheese crust.

CHEESE FOR THE BAKED APPLICATION: MOZZARELLA or MONTERREY JACK are the more common picks — meltier, stretchier, more of a baked-pasta / casserole register. Parmesan works too but reads less traditional for this application. If you want the italian-classical bake, mozzarella. If you want more of an american-comfort register, monterrey jack. Combine both if you can't decide.

=== VARIANT C (STUB / APPENDAGE) — TOMATO PASTE + HEAVY CREAM + LOOSE-LEAF SPINACH ===

Stub. Unspecified vegan/dairy — build on either variant A's or variant B's base, then apply these two additions:

1. TOMATO PASTE + HEAVY CREAM added to the base — pushes the flavor profile toward tomato-cream (vodka-sauce-adjacent) rather than the plain ricotta-and-greens direction of A/B.
2. LOOSE-LEAF SPINACH rather than food-processor-chopped or blended spinach. Whole leaves wilted in rather than dispersed through the base. Reads chunkier and greener; different visual and mouthfeel.

Untested / stub. Log when tried. When tested, decide if variant C should stay unified or split into C-dairy / C-vegan branches.

Raw fresh tomato chopped up and folded into the finished dish works well as a secondary addition. Fresh (not cooked, not canned). Applies to both variants. Skip if you don't have a ripe tomato; not required.

=== SHARED / CROSS-VARIANT NOTES ===

GREENS — REALLY ANYTHING WORKS: spinach, parsley, and mixed greens as the canonical trio (variant A also welcomes parsley + mixed greens; variant B typically just spinach + basil per Beth). Chop/pulse in a food processor before folding in — food-processed greens distribute through the sauce evenly rather than sitting as leafy strands.

DON'T USE A BLENDER — FOOD PROCESSOR, KEEP IT COARSE (BOTH VARIANTS): blenders are wrong for both variants (and for spinach-plus-white-cheese preparations generally) for two reasons:

1. COLOR — NICKELODEON GREEN SLIME: high-shear blending fully ruptures the spinach cells and disperses the chlorophyll evenly through the white cheese (variant A) or tofu-and-cashew (variant B) base. Ends up as a weird pale-green goo that reads un-food-like. Food processor pulses leave spinach in visible flecks against the white base, which reads correct.

2. TEXTURE — KEEP IT COARSE: this sauce should read as ricotta-with-chopped-greens, not as a smooth green sauce. Food processor pulses let you stop at coarse; blender over-smooths. The visible-flecks-of-green + visible-curds-of-cheese texture is what makes it feel like a proper italian ricotta preparation rather than a pureed cream sauce.

If a blender is your only tool: pulse in short bursts and stop early. Expect the color problem regardless.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- lentil-wellington: uses cashews + miso + nutritional yeast in a similar umami stack, but as filling in a savory-baked log rather than as a raw spread. Different application; same underlying vegan-savory principles that variant B here uses.
original_chef: Variant A: mine. Variant B: Beth Hornback (Pass the Plants).
